Uttermost Farthing
UHT-er-mohst FAR-thing
noun
From the saying of Christ in Matthew 5:26; the last and least coin, exacted to the full in judgment.

📖 Biblical Definition

The uttermost farthing is the last and least coin named in the Lord’s warning in the Sermon on the Mount: Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison. Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing. The farthing was a coin of the smallest value, and to pay the uttermost farthing is to discharge the very last and least of a debt, with nothing remitted. The Lord uses the image to press the urgency of reconciliation and the exactness of divine justice: the debtor cast into prison cannot come out until the whole debt, down to the last coin, is paid—and the sinner has no means to pay it. The saying drives home the perfect, exacting righteousness of God, which will not overlook the least transgression, and so the desperate need of the sinner for a Saviour who pays what he cannot. For the believer, Christ has paid the uttermost farthing of his debt upon the cross; for the impenitent, the prison-house of justice exacts payment that can never be made, and so the sentence is endless. The dictionary honors this saying as a window into the exactness of God’s justice and the fulness of Christ’s satisfaction.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The last and least coin in Christ’s warning (Matt 5:26); a figure of the exactness of divine justice, which remits nothing and must be fully paid.

UTTERMOST FARTHING, the last and least coin of Christ’s warning (Mat 5:26).

The debtor cast into prison cannot come out till all is paid.

A figure of the exactness of divine justice, remitting nothing.

The sinner has no means to pay the uttermost farthing.

Christ paid it for the believer; for the impenitent, the debt is endless.

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 5:26 — "Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing."

Mat 18:34 — "And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him."

Col 2:14 — "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;"

Rom 8:1 — "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The saying is softened into mere prudent advice about quarrels; it presses the exact justice of God and the sinner’s need of a Saviour to pay an unpayable debt.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the reduction of the saying to mere prudent counsel about settling disputes out of court, missing its deeper warning. The Lord does urge swift reconciliation, but the image of the debtor who cannot come out of prison till he has paid the uttermost farthing (Matt 5:26) opens upon the exactness of divine justice itself, which will not remit the least transgression unpaid.

The principle to recover is the perfect justice of God and the fulness of Christ’s satisfaction. The unforgiving servant was delivered to the tormentors till he should pay all that was due (Matt 18:34)—and a debt of ten thousand talents can never be paid in prison. So the sinner before God’s exact justice owes a debt he has no means to discharge; the prison-house exacts a payment endless because impossible. But here is the gospel: for the believer, Christ has paid the uttermost farthing, blotting out the handwriting that was against us, nailing it to His cross (Col 2:14), so that there is now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). The exactness of justice magnifies the fulness of grace.
